headline: Hop Aero's Rook rocket promises 550-pound deliveries 750 km in 15 minutes from shipping containers
summary: The Rook rocket, backed by a $1.25M Air Force contract, aims to launch from standard shipping containers and land on unprepared ground. It has not yet flown, with only a small-scale tethered test completed.
details: Hop Aero's 'Rook' autonomous rocket aims to deliver 550 pounds (250 kg) of cargo up to 750 km in approximately 15 minutes. It is designed to launch from a standard 40-foot shipping container and land on unprepared surfaces without a runway.

The Y Combinator startup, with only six employees, has secured a $1.25 million Air Force contract expiring in October. The reference mission for the 15-minute flight is cited as Okinawa to Taiwan, with a potential use for deploying autonomous systems on battlefields.

Preliminary calculations suggest the rocket would reach an altitude of 181 km, well above the Kármán line, meaning it would enter space. The flight profile includes about six to seven minutes of ballistic coast, with the remaining time for boost, reentry, and landing.

While the concept is ambitious, Rook has not yet flown, with only a small-scale prototype completing a tethered test at the Oklahoma spaceport. Other companies like SpaceX (Starship) and Rocket Lab (Neutron) are also working on similar point-to-point delivery concepts with varying progress.

Hop Aero co-founder Jacob Balaj previously worked at Masten Space Systems, which developed vertical takeoff and landing vehicles. Despite ongoing efforts across the industry, no company has yet flown a licensed commercial point-to-point cargo delivery.

headline_marked: [[NASA's Swift rescue spacecraft LINK is in trouble]] with attitude control issues
headline: NASA's Swift rescue spacecraft LINK is in trouble with attitude control issues
summary: NASA's LINK spacecraft, launched to save the Swift observatory from decaying orbit, is now experiencing severe attitude control problems, jeopardizing the mission.
details: NASA's LINK spacecraft, sent to rescue the Swift observatory, is now facing significant issues. Launched in early July, LINK was designed to tug Swift into a higher orbit to extend its operational life. However, the spacecraft recently experienced attitude control problems.

These issues caused LINK to spin uncontrollably, leading to sporadic communication with ground control. The Swift observatory itself is decaying faster than anticipated due to increased solar activity, with re-entry predicted for this year if no intervention occurs.

An update from NASA reveals that two of LINK's three reaction wheels are inoperable, and its cold gas thruster system has lost some functionality. The ground team is currently attempting to stop the spinning using the spacecraft's electric propulsion thrusters.

Once stable, the team must re-establish guidance and navigation to adapt to the new configuration. Only then can Katalyst Space, LINK's builder, and NASA determine if the mission to rescue Swift remains viable, though Katalyst expresses optimism.
